science.title: Organic nitrogen nutrition affects biochemical characteristics, water use efficiency and yield of intercropped barley-chickpea under water stress
science.description: Intercropping and nitrogen (N) management may represent two effective approaches to mitigate the possible effects of water stress. A 2-year field study was conducted to investigate the effects of different N management systems on the biochemical and physiological characteristics, yield, and water use efficiency (WUE) of intercropped barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) and chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.) under water stress during the 2019-20 and 2020-21 growing seasons. The treatments consisted of two irrigation regimes (normal irrigation and irrigation cut-off at the end of flowering), two cropping systems (sole cropping and barley–chickpea intercropping, 1:1 ratio) and three N management systems: organic N nutrition (20 t ha⁻¹ of sheep manure + Azospirillum brasilense), integrated N nutrition (10 t ha⁻¹ of sheep manure + 60 kg N ha⁻¹ + Azospirillum brasilense), and chemical N nutrition (120 kg N ha⁻¹). Regardless of other treatments, water stress significantly reduced most parameters—including grain yield by up to 58.8% in barley and 63.0% in chickpea—except for catalase and peroxidase activities. However, these declining trends were mitigated when organic N nutrition and intercropping were applied. Intercropped chickpea increased chlorophyll b and total chlorophyll content by 32.1 and 52.3%, respectively, compared to sole cropping under water stress. Catalase and peroxidase activities in both crops increased under water stress, particularly under chemical N nutrition in both cropping systems. In intercropping conditions, water stress increased WUE by 1.4% in integrated treatment and by 34.8% in organic, compared to normal irrigation. Overall, considering environmental and climate change concerns, especially in arid climates, barley-chickpea intercropping combined with organic N nutrition can mitigate the severity of water stress and improve grain yield and WUE.
